3- Brep Analysis:

Like the "Evaluate Surface" component, Breps also have similar components that let us extract information and manipulate them.

- Make a simple "Center Box" component.

- Use the "Deconstruct Brep" component to deconstruct the Box into its basic geometries:
1- Faces (surfaces)
2- Edges
3- Vertecies

- Use the "Brep Edges" component to only extract edges.
Note that this component provides few more options relating to the nature of the edges.
Hover the cursor over the OUTPUTS and check them out.

- Use the "Brep Wireframe" component to only extract edges. This is similar to the "Deconstruct Brep"'s Edges OUTPUT.

- Check out the "Shape In Brep" and see how it can be useful to you.

5- Brep Operations 2:

Other operations are also present, which apply to whole Breps, or involve intersections between Breps/Curves or Breps/Breps.

- Check out the following components and check what is needed for each in order to see their actions:

- "Brep / Line"
- "Brep / Brep"
- "Trim Solid"
- "Solid Union"
- "Solid Difference"
- "Solid Intersection"
- "Box Slits"


Boolean Union (in Rhino) Vs. Solid Union (in Grasshopper)

4- Brep Operations 1:

Grasshopper provides many useful components to manipulate Breps. We will see below few useful ones.

- Based on the previous Definition on the left, use the following components and check what is needed for each in order to see their actions:

- "Brep Join"
- "Cap Holes"

9- Triangulation:

Some of the interesting components in Grasshopper that provide complex geometry are triangulation operators, such as Delaunay and Voronoi.

Let's checkout few Delaunay and Voronoi components below and see the required inouts and resultants.

6- Mesh:

Similarly to Primitive Breps, basic Meshes can also be constructed within Grasshopper.

Check out the following components and what is needed to feed them:

- "Mesh Box"
- "Mesh Sphere"


In addition to making Meshes from scratch, Grasshopper provides few components that let you convert Breps into Meshes, like the following components:

- "Mesh Brep"
- "Simple Mesh"

7- Mesh Analysis:

Similarly to the Brep Analysis components, Meshes also have Analysis components that help analyze and extract important information from Meshes in order to manipulate them parametrically.

- Check out the following components and what is needed to feed them:

- "Mesh Edges"
- "Deconstruct Mesh"
- "Deconstruct Face"
- "Face Normals"
- "Mesh Explode"

8- Mesh Operations:

Again, similarly to Brep operations, Grasshopper provides useful components to manipulate Meshes.

- Check out the following components and what is needed to feed them:

- "Mesh Union"
- "Mesh Difference"
- "Mesh Intersection"

- "Mesh Smooth"
- "Triangulate"
- "Quadrangulate"

1- NURBS & Mesh: What are they?

NURBS:

"Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines) are mathematical representations that can accurately model any shape from a simple 2D line, circle, arc, or box to the most complex 3D free-form organic surface or solid. Because of their flexibility and accuracy, NURBS models can be used in any process from illustration and animation to manufacturing."

Source:
http://grasshopperprimer.com/en/1-foundations/1-5/1_surface-geometry.html

Mesh:

"In the field of computational modeling, meshes are one of the most pervasive forms of representing 3D geometry. Mesh geometry can be a light-weight and flexible alternative to working with NURBS, and are used in everything from rendering and visualizations to digital fabrication and 3D printing."

"A Mesh is a collection of quadrilaterals and triangles that represent a surface or solid geometry."
A mesh is composed of "vertices, edges, and faces, as well as additional mesh properties such as colors and normals."

"Meshes can be favorable in situations where:

There must be a dynamically updated rendering of a form that is changing in shape but not in face connectivity
A discretized approximation of a curved geometry would suffice
A low-resolution geometry must be systematically smoothed (or articlated) using computational methods to arrive at a higher-resolution model.
The low resolution model must be able to be to simultaneously support local, high resolution detail
Meshes can be unfavorable in situations where:

Curvature and smoothness must be represented with a high level of precision
True derivatives must be evaluated
The geometry must be converted into a manufacturable solid
The final form must be able to be easily edited manually"

Sources:
http://grasshopperprimer.com/en/1-foundations/1-6/0_Getting%20Started%20with%20Meshes.html
http://grasshopperprimer.com/en/1-foundations/1-6/1_What%20is%20a%20Mesh.html
http://grasshopperprimer.com/en/1-foundations/1-6/2_Understanding%20Topology.html

NURBS & Mesh:

Grasshopper provides various tools to work with both NURBS & Meshes.

Unless otherwise specified, solids & Breps in Grasshopper are NURBS geometry. When a Mesh is being used, it usually states that it is a "Mesh" and its icon shows small squarish meshes.

Below on the left are Geometry generation and analysis components for NURBS (can also be found under the tab "Surface")

On the right, Mesh components (can also be found under the tab "Mesh")

2- Brep: What is it?

"The word Brep stands for Boundary Representation. That in itself doesn't tell you much, but allow me to break down the general idea behind Breps. In Rhino UI itself, we don't use the word Brep, that one is only for programmers. Instead "Polysurface" is used, but it is not an ideal replacement because a Brep may well have only a single surface."
- David Rutten

Source:

http://www.grasshopper3d.com/forum/topics/how-to-make-a-brep

- In Grasshopper, a Brep is a NURBS goemetry, and not a Mesh.

What is modeled in Rhino is a Surface or a Polysurface or a Mesh.

When a Polysurface is being referenced in Grasshopper, it would be called as a Brep and not a polysurface.

- The "Mesh Brep" component converts a Brep into a Mesh.

"NOTE: it is generally much easier to convert from a NURBS geometry to a mesh object rather than the other way around. While the UV coordinates of a NURBS surface are straightforward to convert to quad faces of a mesh, the opposite is not necessarily true, since a mesh might contain a combination of triangles and quads in a way that is not simple to extract a UV coordinate system out of."

Source:
http://grasshopperprimer.com/en/1-foundations/1-6/3_Creating%20Meshes.html
